title: Senior's toolkit: cleaning data
summary: Find missing values, duplicates and bad types fast, fix them on purpose, and check what each fix changed.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: cleaning data
steps.body: Cleaning is most of the job. The skill is not only fixing values but knowing how many rows each fix touched, so nothing disappears silently. These are the calls analysts use every day.

toolkit.what: Missing values per column. `.mean()` instead of `.sum()` gives the share, which is easier to judge.
Drop rows missing what you really need. A bare `dropna()` drops a row if *any* column is empty, which often loses most of the data.
flags: drop only rows that are completely empty
keep rows with at least 5 values

toolkit.what: Fill gaps with a value that is correct for the business, per column. `ffill` carries the last value forward (for readings over time). `fillna(method=...)` is deprecated.
flags: fill at most 2 gaps in a row

toolkit.what: Find duplicates. `keep=False` marks every copy, so you can look at all of them before you decide which to keep.
Turn text into numbers; anything that does not parse becomes NaN. Always look at what was coerced.
flags: bad values become NaN instead of raising
the default: fail on the first bad value
the same for dates, with the format stated

toolkit.what: Store a column with few distinct values as a category: much less memory, and it documents the allowed values.
flags: real text (pandas 3 uses a string dtype by default)
a fixed, ordered set such as S < M < L

toolkit.what: Vectorised string methods. Normalise keys before you compare, group or deduplicate them.
flags: a mask that treats missing as False

steps.prompt: After `df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["amount"], errors="coerce")` the revenue total dropped by 15%. What should you have done?
options: Look at what was coerced first: `raw[pd.to_numeric(raw, errors="coerce").isna() & raw.notna()]`. Values such as `"1,250.00"` need fixing (remove the comma), not deleting
Nothing: rows that do not parse are always junk
Multiply the total by 1.15 to correct it
steps.explain: `coerce` hides problems by design. Listing the original values that became NaN shows whether they are junk or a format you can fix. Here thousands separators were turning real sales into NaN. (`errors="ignore"` is deprecated and just hands back the text column unchanged.)

steps.prompt: `customers.drop_duplicates(subset="email")` still leaves the same person twice: `Ann@Shop.com ` and `ann@shop.com`. What is the fix?
options: Normalise first, `df["email"] = df["email"].str.strip().str.lower()`, then drop duplicates
steps.explain: Duplicates are found by exact equality. Case and a trailing space make the strings different. Clean the key, then deduplicate, then count how many rows that removed.

steps.prompt: Match each argument to its meaning.
pairs: mark every copy of a duplicate
treat missing values as not matching

steps.prompt: Normalise the email column, then show every row whose email appears more than once.
steps.explain: pandas follows Python's names: `strip` and `lower`. `keep=False` marks all copies; `"first"` (the default) would not mark the first one.
`"n/a"` and `"1,200"` do not parse, and `None` was already missing. Only one of them (`"n/a"`) is real junk: `"1,200"` is a sale that needs its comma removed.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Print the row count before and after every cleaning step, and look at the rows a fix touches (`keep=False`, the values `coerce` turned into NaN) before you accept it. Normalise keys with `.str` methods before you deduplicate, join or group on them.
